title: #14 Patrik Wahlén on Business Adventures
summary:
I think it's so common that people take risks to make money. that they take even more risk, lending even more money, raising the bets. And I think there is something about risk and risk management and people in general that we
could learn from that story.

notes: Patrik Wahlén is the Co-Founder and Chairman of the Swedish industrial group Volati. We have the pleasure to discuss one of his favorite books, featuring several timeless Wall Street stories. Besides the lessons from John Brooks and the stock market, we talk about how to build a lasting serial acquirer and what you can learn from English soccer clubs. The episode was recorded on December 20, 2021. For more info about the podcast, go to the episode page . ————————————— Episode Chapters Part 1: Lessons from Business Adventures (00:00) Intro to Patrik Wahlén and ”Business Adventures” (01:56) Buffett’s AMEX investment and risks (04:13) Lessons from the first flash crash (05:43) Patrik’s most common biases (06:25) Big bets: Ford’s Edsel failure (09:44) Diversification and philanthropy: Xerox (12:51) Overconfidence and frugality: Clarence Saunders (15:34) Finding your passion: David Lilienthal Part 2: Building a Lasting Serial Acquirer (16:27) Patrik Wahlén and Volati (17:57) Building a lasting serial acquirer (28:10) Lessons from soccer (30:54) Book recommendations ————————————— Books Mentioned Business Adventures - John Brooks (1969) Confusion of Confusions - Joseph de la Vega (1688) Expectations Investing - Michael Mauboussin & Alfred Rappaport (2021) The House of Morgan - Ron Chernow (1990) All books by Peter Bevelin ————————————— Companies Mentioned (in order of its first appearance) Volati American Express Ford Xerox Piggly Wiggly Tornum (part of Volati) Assa Abloy Nibe Salix (part of Volati) ————————————— More on Patrik Wahlén Twitter: https://twitter.com/PGWahlen Volati: https://www.volati.se/en/about-volati.aspx ————————————— What is Investing by the Books? Investing by the Books was founded by Henrik Andersson, Bo Börtemark, Mats Larsson and Michael Persson. It has published hundreds of book reviews in the past 10 years and operates on a non-profit basis. Visit the website: http://www.investingbythebooks.com/ Follow on Twitter: https://twitter.com/Investbythebook ————————————— What is Redeye? Welcome to Investing by the Books, a podcast by Red Eye.
I'm your host, Eddie Palmyan, and next to me in the studio is my friend Niklas Saevos.
How are you today?
I'm great. I had a great weekend, and I'm really, really excited to speak to our guest today.
Yeah, today we have the great pleasure of talking to Patrick Valen,
co-founder and chairman of the Swedish industrial group Volati, listed on Nastak, Stockholm.
Valen is both a successful businessman and a big reader.
And for today's episode, he has picked the book Business Adventures,
12 classic tales from the world of Wall Street, written by you.
John Brooks, published in 1969, and quoted by Bill Gates as The Best Business Book I've
ever read. Here comes our conversation with Patrick Valje. Welcome to the studio, Patrick.
Thank you very much. So, Patrick, how did your interest in business and investing start?
Well, I've been interested in business for all my life for as long as I can remember. Investing,
I'm a late bloomer into. I started to get interested in that during my time at university,
actually. And why have you chosen the book Business Adventures? I think it's
It's a great book. It's a bit off the beaten track, even if Bill Gates and Warren Buffett likes it.
I think it's lots of good stories that you can learn a lot about from.
Yeah. And when was the first time you read it? I think it's like 10 years ago. I picked it up from
from reading about Bill Gates, recommended it on his, on his page. I had not heard about the book
before, so I'm really happy that you chose this book. And the author is, you chose this book. And the
author is John Brooks, as Eddie said. Can you tell us a little bit about him?
Yeah, he's a writer or was a writer and a journalist. He was contributed to the New Yorker.
And he was gradually writing more and more about Wall Street and business. But his background was
like a, we would like to be an author and turned into a journalist.
The book is structured in 12 chapters and in my view, they can be read separately.
I would divide the chapters into three segments, business, the financial industry,
and policy. And having followed you on Twitter and what you have done with Volati, I know that
you're interested in all three segments. So, do you have a favorite chapter?
It's varies, which chapter is my favorite. I reread the book in for this, and I found the chapter
about the oil scandal, which led up to Warren Buffett's famous investment in Amex to be extra
fascinating this time. And why was that? Because I got even more impressed of Warren Buffett's
investment reading about the oil scandal.
from a different perspective. This scandal was so huge that it actually affected Wall Street in general.
And thinking about war and making this big bet at Amex when they were down like 50% made me even more impressed.
And also, I think there is something about this guy. I don't remember his name. What was his name?
The Angeles.
Exactly. I think it's so common that people take risks to make money. They don't succeed, but they're so secure of their own ideas.
that they take even more risk, lending even more money, raising the bets.
And he did that a couple of times.
And he did it first in Chicago.
And they said, this is enough.
You can't trade here anymore.
And then he turned to New York and did it again.
And I think there is something about risk and risk management and people in general that we
could learn from that story.
Sounds like sunk cost fallacy.
You just keep investing in something even though it doesn't work out.
Yeah.
And that really put the whole stock exchange at risk in this situation.
One quote that I really liked was more than money was at stake.
It was a question of the relation of the stock exchange to the country's many million investors.
One thing we will get back to, I think, is some of the similarities, I think, got repeated a bit in the financial crisis, even though it was bigger, of course.
Do you have any thoughts on that?
Do you think it was a similar situation?
People take too much risk.
And when things goes good, they raise their bets because they think there are gods that could do everything.
And if they go bad, they raise their bets.
gets to sort of hide their losses.
You see that time and time again.
A common theme in the book for me is about trust, which comes back all the time.
And one other timeless story is the chapter on fluctuations of the market where Brooks writes that the New York Stock
Exchange is a sociological test tube forever contributing to the human species of self-understanding.
So what are your thoughts about that?
I think that chapter is lovely.
And I think it's lovely that he's.
have citations from a book from 1688 about Amsterdam stock exchange.
And when you're reading those, I think they're timeless.
I think that's very fascinating.
Can you tell our listeners a bit about that story, about the fluctuations on the market?
This was 1962, if I remember, right?
The market has been going up for many years.
And suddenly, the market gets a bit nervous, and they start to sell off.
And in like three days, they are selling off the market.
at like 25%. And then suddenly it turns back. And if you have been asleep for those
three days, you wouldn't have noticed that anything have changed. And it's all about the market or
the participants in the market thinking about what will everybody else do. So first, they think that
everyone will sell and then they are selling, selling everything. And when the market goes down
to 500, there is an idea that it could never go below 500. And then suddenly everyone
starts to buy. I think that's timeless. That happens again.
and again. And the market goes back to zero, more or less at the end of the week.
Exactly. I think that's very fascinating. The first flash crash.
And on the topic of self-understanding, what would you say are your most common biases?
Oh, I have so many. I think all of us have the most of them and we think that we could control them.
But if I divide it into two segments, one, which is how I act within Volati and one,
which is how I act on the outside of Volati. I would say that outside Volati, I would say that
outside Volati, I trust my guts too much. I don't do my homework. I just act on use and run
with the herd, and I do that again and again. So what I actually have done is decided to not do too many
investments outside Volati because I'm not particularly good at it. You're staying in your circle of
competence. That's a very good nice way to put it. In the second chapter, we read about Ford's launch
launch of the Edselcar. And this is really an American anti-success story that takes place
the late 1950s. So what are the lessons from this failure?
There is so many lessons. I think we can learn a lot about the market economy is very good in
correcting mistakes. So they did this huge investments, like $300 million, if I remember right.
And in just a couple of years of time, they quit it to stop manufacturing and selling the car.
Imagine this happening in a commander economy. They will continue for years and years and
years, giving customers cast I didn't like, just because that's the way command
economy works.
So market economies is fascinating and a great, great thing.
So that's one lesson.
Another lesson more from an investment's perspective is, so this is the Ford company, huge company,
and they are so convinced that they will move into a big new market and that they will make
lots of money from it. And they fail. They fail so badly. And I'm thinking about if I was
reading about this car at the time and all the money they spent on it and how sure they are about their
success, wouldn't I like to buy that stock just to get into that? And I think we can learn a lot about that,
about how to listen to managers, to be careful about their predictions, about the future
and stuff like that.
And why do you think they failed?
That's a very good question.
I think they failed.
I think big bets is something you should be aware of.
So they made a huge bet and they got it wrong.
Maybe it's better to make more smaller bets and hedge your bets.
That's a bit contrary to Buffett's and Munger's concentration and bet big when you have the chance.
Yes, but that's in a different context, I would say.
So if you are a manager and you need to develop new products, the future is
so unsure that you maybe should think more in bets. And when you have a success, then you start
to invest more heavily in it.
So you mean there's the difference between an operating investment and an actual, like, to buy stock
in a company?
I think that's a big different situations.
My takeaway from the chapter with Edsel is more or less that they had to invest a lot.
I mean, Ford had to invest a lot in their manufacturing and.
advertising and so on.
And for maybe a modern company today, they can maybe do a small beta test before and really don't make
that huge investment beforehand.
What's your view on that?
I think it's right, but it's not a complete truth.
I think if you look at many of the companies, Google's or Microsoft or Facebook,
or whatever, they make great investments.
I think the companies today even make larger investments than we did
previously in different kinds of things, but still huge bets.
So maybe you're right, but I think it's still companies making huge bets.
And Nokia, which Microsoft acquired, could be a good example of a bet going wrong.
Yeah, definitely true.
Another theme that is connected to this is the story of Xerox.
They really bet big on one thing, while the largest companies today, the tech
companies, for example, they seem to make bets all over the place.
And some become huge successes and make up for all the bad choices they do.
Syracus is very fascinating because they bet early on that they got it right.
But then when they were successful, they had lots of investments in research and development,
and they didn't trust their own findings.
So actually, Microsoft and Apple, is, took their ideas from Xerox because they didn't carry it out.
That's really interesting point.
Yeah, and I love the title.
Syrox, four of them. I think that's the most brilliant headline ever.
The copy company.
So what other lessons do you have from that story?
I think there is so many things.
When I read that chapter, I was thinking, what would my picture of Syrox be if I was
reading this in the mid-60s. So successful, so strong cash flows, dominating a new market,
which is growing very rapidly, I was thinking that they will be a huge success for a very long time.
And today, we don't think about them in that way, do we? When you are in the middle of something,
the companies that are driving is doing all the good things, they will eventually run into
problems, most of them. I think that's a very big lesson.
So you need to stay long-term and look.
far into the future?
You have to look far into the future, but also realize that the future is very unpredictable.
So diversification.
Exactly.
I think it was funny because I'm more or less, I've mostly heard about the downfall of Xerox, not the success,
but of course you need a success before you can get a downfall.
So I was really interested about the story because it seems like Xerox in their successful
years didn't only focus on the business.
They also focused on like philanthropic.
matters and so on. So I wanted to ask you as a business leader, how do you think businesses
shall consider society? I think if you should be long-term successful as a business, you have to have
happy customers, happy suppliers, happy employees, and happy society in general. Otherwise,
you are not successful in the long run, so that's important. But with that said, I don't think
that boards or management, they always have.
to face up to the owners. So they have to be very careful with the money. And I was surprised
reading about Xerox, even sort of sponsoring UN. I think that is a step too far maybe. And I also thinking
that, reading about that, sponsoring universities and stuff like that, that's very good. But it also
changes the focus from the management. And I felt that Syrox was so successful that they moved
their focus from the business into society. And I think that was maybe
one step into the downfall, actually.
Another interesting chapter tells the story of Clarence Saunders, the pigly-wiggly-wiggly stores that he's created, and he was basically the inventor of the modern supermarket concept with aisles where people could walk and check out their groceries.
But he was mostly famous for the chapter here, where he was doing a corner on Wall Street.
So for those who don't remember, this was in the 1920s, what is a corner?
A corner is when you buy all the stocks in the market to make sure that.
that short sellers can't cover their position.
And how was this story built up?
This story is lovely. It's like Michael Lewis, all his stories. So it's great characters.
And this businessman is running a business. He finds out that the big guys in Wall Street is shortening
his stock and he thinks that, wow, I will outsmart them. And he starts to buy the stock.
He buys everything. And he's quite clever, actually.
And in the beginning, it looks like that he will be successful and that he will make loads some money.
And then, of course, there is this turn of the story that the stock exchange gives them four days extra to cover their positions.
And they find the stocks.
And suddenly his corner is gone and he loses quite a lot of money.
And he goes bankrupt, actually.
Yeah, it's hard to squeeze out the bears.
It's very hard.
And you shouldn't fight with the big guys.
I'm always thinking about.
at the stock markets like the Super Bowl. And I have this pink speedos and these guys is running
towards me. And that's the market. That's Mr. Market coming for you. And you should be pretty sure
that you could run fast. It didn't have any lessons from the market before. It seemed like a real
businessman, not really knowing the rules of the game, so to speak. No. And in the beginning
it works. I think there's a lesson as well. You don't always have to play by the
rules. You could invent them by yourself. But you should be aware of the big guys.
and also he was very emotional. I mean, he was aggressive and he was mostly
he didn't like the Wall Street at all and he wanted to take them down.
He goes overconfident. He thinks that he has success and he keeps carrying on.
Quite interesting also that he had a success afterwards as well.
Again, he came back.
But then he failed again, right?
That's an entrepreneur.
Yeah. Yeah, I could, I mean, if he had been frugal on the side, then maybe he would have
been a success. They discuss a lot about the pink palace, and I think there is some documentary about
that pink palace, his huge mansion with a private golf course and so on.
He wanted to live a very luxurious life that he didn't really, couldn't afford. And related
to that is chapter nine about David Lilliantal, a former politician. He started a second life,
as the chapter is named. He became a successful entrepreneur and financially independent by far.
And he says in that chapter that he doesn't think money makes much difference as long as you have enough.
So what is your view on that?
Completely correct.
That's the way it is.
And I think my takeaway from that story is that you always have to find what you really like to do.
He was very successful from the beginning.
It seems to have lots of fun what he was doing and enjoying it.
And then second life, it was the same.
It was not focusing on the money.
It was focusing in doing a good job, learning, improving.
I think that's the way to do it. If you focus on the money, it will not be successful.
You always have to try to learn and improve. I think that's a very big lesson.
And how have you find, like, what is meaningful for you?
For me, I love what I'm doing. I really love what I'm doing, building a company, trying to build
something sustainable for a very long time, and building something which is independent
independent from myself, building something that have success in the walls. I think
that's tremendous fun. How has it helped you to be two running the company from the start?
I think it's very good to be two, or even for many years we have been four, maybe, with Morton and
Matthias, our CEO and CFO. They have left us now, are still with us, but into those positions.
I think different perspectives is very important. I think trying to find a partner
partner which looks at life some ways like you, but also have different perspectives. I think
that's been very helpful.
And for those who are not familiar with Volati, what kind of company is it?
So we started Volati 2003, Karl Palagin and I, and we had an idea of acquiring companies.
Generational shifts was a big thing at that time. And we thought, let's buy some companies
and see if we could build a group of companies. So that was the way we started.
Today, we are 6 billion Swedish in turnover. We have an EBTA margin of 10%.
to return on equity of 33, if I remember right.
And we have been growing the last 12 months with like 50% EBTA per share, but over the long

That's a very good, very good question.
Delayed gratification seems to.
seems to work quite well.
I think it's, I have not been driven about the money.
Money is important, but if you have enough, you have enough.
I have always tried to build something, to build something lasting.
I think that's the fun thing of this.
Do you have an aim with that building?
I mean, do you, do you want your kids and so on to take up the helm where you were you left
in the Andor?
That would be lovely.
But more important is,
I have some idea that when I'm 85, I will walk into the office, have a cup of coffee with the guys running the business and talk with them.
I think that would be lovely.
So it's building something lasting.
That's my dream.
Sounds really nice.
I wanted to go into the type of company you're running.
Many speak about serial acquires.
You call yourself an industry group.

that carry a large premium to the private companies that they acquire.

And I wanted to hear your take on how fragile a serial acquire is from the start and how important

There is many things in that question.
If I should start with the end, I think the first acquisition is crucial.
So if we had made a mistake acquiring to honor first acquisition, I wouldn't be sitting here.
That's true. And that's more luck than skill.
But also starting with the first part of the question around valuation, I think there
is some interesting stuff there.
First of all, I think you should think about larger companies often carry.
There is a higher valuation than a smaller one, so that is in play here.
Also, we have liquidity, so a listed company has a higher price versus a non-listed company.
So that you should think about.
But also, you had Michael on the pod.
Michael Mobosan.
Yeah, I think his book is very fascinating.
So if we try to do this here, so how could this company motivate this valuation?
And I think that's all about the return on invested capital and the growth.
rate. So some of parts gives you in one direction, but the other direction would be to look at

has a low growth rate, although they have a good capital return. So what you basically do

The duration is really key there because, I mean, in the, I mean, if you take the valuation now,

What is your strategy to achieve that?
I think making the company independent of yourself and trying to make the company independent of yourself and trying to
make the lessons you have learned into.
rules and processes and checklists and whatever. Also to figure out what
you have been good or lucky at doing that is not able to transfer to other people and trying to find

I think changing business models is very important for every company growing. So what we

creating. So how do you think about serial acquires trying to grow really
quickly through either raising equity and or debt? What's your take on that?
I think that's a very important point to think about. I think you always have to look into the return
on invested capital. I think that's crucial. I think too many people today is just looking into
EBTA growth, not even EBTA per share.
as such, I think that's a big mistake. So I think that's a very important lesson.
And about depth, I think, especially right now, you should be very careful about the level of depth the
that companies says very important. And you're not scared yourself about when a company such as
yours is growing, the absolute number of depth will increase. Actually, I think Volati has had
at too low level of depth since our IPO. I think we have, if I remember right,
1.7 net debt at the moment and we're aiming for being between two and three. So we are
quite conservative. We have long durations. So, okay, the absolute number is quite high, but
in relation to the business is not that high. And also when you are growing, you get more
diversified, you get less risk. And also you get more important towards the banks.
So no, I'm not, no, the short answer is no. Good answer. Another question is that
that people around us internationally see is how many serial acquirers and holding companies we have
in Sweden that are also many of them really successful and have been successful for a long time.
I'm curious to know, why do you think that is? I think there is two parts to that. One is,
like when we started 2003, 2003, there was not so many of them. But lately, some have been
very successful and success always attracts copycats, if I could use that word. And should everyone
be aware of that when you find an attractive investment, it will attract capital and the returns will

industry which has plenty of small companies and quite a lot of large companies, but not so much in
between. So what is happening is that mid-sized companies is acquiring small-sized
companies, so the structure is quite good for this type of business.
And do you think Swedish companies and entrepreneurs get less fame than they deserve?
I think that entrepreneurs should strive for success, not fame.
And what do you see as the pros and cons of being a generalist in the type of companies that you buy
compared to niche players like Asabloi or Niebu?
I think we are trying to be both at the moment, actually. I think niche players,
I talked before about synergies and the need to add value as an owner.
I think too much emphasis is on acquiring and making the arbitrage.
I think you had to add value as an owner in this market, and it's easy to do that as a niche player.
So I would say that we are working in a couple of niches to be able to do that.
With that said, being a generalist creates opportunities to hit the big elephant
when that opportunities arise.
At this, in this particular time, I would say it's hard to find an elephant, but markets is changing.
So who knows, in a couple of years, there will be a good chance to do something a bit different.
And you said before that you're building these groups of companies and cluster them together.
How does that help you when you meet entrepreneurs who maybe wants to sell to someone
who really knows their business?
I think it works two ways, actually.
So it's beneficial because you understand the business.
You maybe know each other for a long time.
You know which questions to ask.
That's good.
But many entrepreneurs would like their company to live on with their own name and don't.
I'm synergies sounds good, but if you're the seller, it sounds bad.
So it works both ways.
But we have been quite successful in Solix, which is a supplier to the building industry, finding synergies,
building a platform for growing the companies that we're acquiring.
The same within labels.
I think you could do it.
It's pros and coins.
It's an incredible company you have created over quite a short space of time.
But moving on from the company side a bit, I know that you have a huge interest in soccer
